slides.title: Topology

slides.html:
A Naive Question

What does it mean for two spaces to be "essentially the same"?

  • a rubber band: circle ≅ square, but ≠ "8"
  • coffee mug ≅ doughnut, ≠ ball
  • topological invariants: connectedness, compactness, components after deleting a point ⟹ show non-homeomorphic
  • homotopy invariants: winding number ⟹ decide whether two maps can be deformed into each other

Integers cannot change continuously — the core of every existence proof here.
slides.title: A Naive Question

slides.html: 1. Metric Spaces and Homeomorphisms
slides.title: 1. Metric Spaces and Homeomorphisms

slides.html:
Proving Non-Homeomorphism: Delete a Point

f a homeomorphism ⟹ X\setminus\{p\}\cong Y\setminus\{f(p)\}

  • (0,1)\not\cong S^1: disconnected vs connected after deleting a point
  • three-petal flower \not\cong S^1: deleting the common point leaves 3 components
  • (0,1)\cup(1,2)\cong(0,1)\cup(2,3), \not\cong(0,1)
  • [0,1]\not\cong(0,1): compactness
slides.title: Proving Non-Homeomorphism: Delete a Point

slides.html:
Embeddings and Famous Theorems

  • embedding: injective + homeomorphism onto the image; isotopy: continuous deformation of embeddings
  • Jordan curve theorem: S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^2 splits the plane in two
  • Schoenflies: the embedding extends to a homeomorphism of the plane
  • Alexander horned sphere: a wild embedding S^2\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^3
  • Peano curve: a continuous surjection I\to I^2
  • Brouwer: f:D^n\to D^n has a fixed point
slides.title: Embeddings and Famous Theorems

slides.html: 2–3. Topological Spaces and Closure
slides.title: 2–3. Topological Spaces and Closure

slides.html:
Closure and Accumulation Points

x\in\overline A\iff every neighbourhood of x meets A

  • \overline A=A\cup A'; A=\{-1\}\cup(0,1): A'=[0,1]
  • metric spaces: accumulation point ⟺ sequential limit
  • sequences fail in general topology: [0,1] with the cocountable topology, 0\in(0,1]' yet no sequence converges to 0
slides.title: Closure and Accumulation Points

slides.html: 4–5. Continuity and Compactness
slides.title: 4–5. Continuity and Compactness

slides.html:
Continuous Maps (Open-Set Version)

f continuous ⟺ preimages of open sets are open ⟺ preimages of closed sets are closed ⟺ f(\overline A)\subseteq\overline{f(A)}

  • f(x)=1/x: f(\overline X)\subsetneq\overline{f(X)}, inclusion not equality
  • pasting lemma for finite closed covers; not for infinite ones
slides.title: Continuous Maps (Open-Set Version)

slides.html:
Extreme Values and Heine–Borel

  • X non-empty compact, f continuous ⟹ attains max and min
  • I^n is compact (repeated bisection)
  • Heine–Borel: in \mathbb R^n, compact ⟺ closed and bounded
  • metric spaces: compact ⟺ sequentially compact
  • in general: compact ⟺ every family of closed sets with the finite intersection property has non-empty intersection
slides.title: Extreme Values and Heine–Borel

slides.html: 6–7. Baire and Fixed Points
slides.title: 6–7. Baire and Fixed Points

slides.html:
Application: Continuous Nowhere Differentiable Functions

A_n=\{f\in C(I):\exists x\,\forall y,\ |f(y)-f(x)|\le n|y-x|\}
  • A_n is closed: uniform limit + compactness of I gives x_k\to x
  • A_n has empty interior: piecewise-linear approximation + a high-frequency triangle wave with slopes above M+n
  • a finite derivative ⟹ f\in A_n for some n
  • ⟹ continuous functions with no finite derivative exist, and are dense in C(I)
slides.title: Application: Continuous Nowhere Differentiable Functions

slides.html:
The Banach Contraction Principle

complete + d(Tx,Ty)\le q\,d(x,y), q<1 ⟹ unique fixed point, iteration converges

  • d(x_{n+1},x_n)\le q^nd(x_1,x_0) ⟹ Cauchy
  • uniqueness: d\le q\,d ⟹ d=0
slides.title: The Banach Contraction Principle

slides.html:
Local Existence and Uniqueness for ODEs

x'=f(x,t),\ x(t_0)=x_0, f uniformly Lipschitz in x (constant L)

(Tx)(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^tf(x(s),s)\,ds,\quad\|Tx-Ty\|\le L\varepsilon\|x-y\|
  • with L\varepsilon<1 ⟹ unique solution on a short interval
  • extension to the whole interval needs piecewise continuation (fine under a global Lipschitz bound)
slides.title: Local Existence and Uniqueness for ODEs

slides.html:
The Inverse Function Theorem

Df(x_0) invertible ⟹ f|_U:U\to V is a C^1 diffeomorphism, Dg(y)=[Df(g(y))]^{-1}

  • contraction: T_y(x)=x-A(f(x)-y), A=[Df(x_0)]^{-1}
  • DT_y(x_0)=0 ⟹ derivative norm <1 on a small ball
  • the derivative of the inverse must be evaluated at the right point
slides.title: The Inverse Function Theorem

slides.html: 8–9. Connectedness and the Cantor Set
slides.title: 8–9. Connectedness and the Cantor Set

slides.html:
Connectedness

  • separation: non-empty disjoint open U,V with X=U\cup V; no separation = connected
  • continuous images are connected; intermediate value property
  • path connected ⟹ connected; convex sets are path connected
  • open subsets of \mathbb R^n: connected ⟺ path connected
  • components: C_x the largest connected subset, closed, pairwise disjoint
slides.title: Connectedness

slides.html:
Antoine's Necklace

  • the intersection of interlocking solid tori: a Cantor set in \mathbb R^3
  • its complement is not simply connected
  • homeomorphic as abstract spaces, yet the embeddings can differ
slides.title: Antoine's Necklace

slides.html: 10–11. Homotopy and Winding Numbers
slides.title: 10–11. Homotopy and Winding Numbers

slides.html:
Homotopy

f\simeq g: H:X\times I\to Y, H_0=f,\ H_1=g

  • an equivalence relation (symmetry: 1-t; transitivity: concatenation with 2t)
  • compatible with composition
  • null-homotopic: homotopic to a constant; convex target ⟹ straight-line homotopy
  • boundary obstruction: F:D^2\to\mathbb R^2 nowhere zero ⟹ F|_{S^1} null-homotopic (H=F((1-t)z))
slides.title: Homotopy

slides.html:
A Homotopy Invariant — and a Complete One

f\simeq g\iff W(f,0)=W(g,0), \ [S^1,\mathbb C^*]\cong\mathbb Z; f null-homotopic ⟺ W=0

  • ⟹: homotopy lifting; \dfrac{\widetilde H(1,t)-\widetilde H(0,t)}{2\pi i} integer-valued and continuous ⟹ constant
  • ⟸: L=(1-t)\widetilde f+t\widetilde g descends to a homotopy
  • perturbation test: |f-g|<|f| ⟹ same winding number
slides.title: A Homotopy Invariant — and a Complete One

slides.html: 12. Applications of the Winding Number
slides.title: 12. Applications of the Winding Number
No Retraction to the Boundary; Brouwer

slides.html:
Retractions and the Integral Formula

  • retraction r:X\to A, r|_A=\mathrm{id}; strong deformation retract: H(a,t)=a. For S^1\subset\mathbb C^*: H=(1-t)z+tz/|z|, so [Y,S^1]\cong[Y,\mathbb C^*]
  • W(\gamma,0)=\dfrac1{2\pi i}\oint\dfrac{dz}z=\dfrac1{2\pi}\int\dfrac{x\,dy-y\,dx}{x^2+y^2}
  • \arctan(y/x) is not a global argument; \omega is closed but not exact
slides.title: Retractions and the Integral Formula

slides.html:
Counting Zeros

F=\prod(z-z_j)\,g, |z_j|<1, g\ne0 ⟹ W(F|_{S^1},0)=n

  • on the boundary (z-tz_j)\to z is a homotopy; g|_{S^1} is null-homotopic
  • holomorphic case: \dfrac1{2\pi i}\oint\dfrac{F'}F\,dz = number of zeros inside (argument principle)
  • a general continuous function cannot use multiplicities unconditionally
slides.title: Counting Zeros

slides.html: 13. Vector Fields and the Hairy Ball Theorem
slides.title: 13. Vector Fields and the Hairy Ball Theorem

slides.html:
The Hairy Ball Theorem

Every continuous tangent vector field on S^2 has a zero.

  • two projections h_S,h_N, transition w\mapsto1/\bar w
  • on the equator v\mapsto-e^{2i\theta}\bar v
  • no zero ⟹ both winding numbers are 0
  • but W(V_S)=2-W(V_N) ⟹ 0=2, contradiction
slides.title: The Hairy Ball Theorem

slides.html:
Poincaré–Hopf and a Map of Methods

\sum_{V(x)=0}\mathrm{ind}_x(V)=\chi(S^2)=2
To prove Method
not homeomorphic delete a point, compactness, connectedness
existence Baire; contraction principle
a root / fixed point / zero exists winding number by contradiction: build a non-vanishing map
two maps homotopic straight-line homotopy; winding number
slides.title: Poincaré–Hopf and a Map of Methods

slides.html:
Common Pitfalls

  1. the inverse of a continuous bijection need not be continuous
  2. the sequential characterisation holds only for metric spaces
  3. "closed and bounded ⟹ compact" only in \mathbb R^n
  4. nowhere dense ≠ empty interior
  5. connected ≠ path connected
  6. the argument is not a global function on the punctured plane; winding numbers depend on orientation conventions
slides.title: Common Pitfalls
